title: Preamble, Fundamental Rights and Duties

cards.h: The Constitution's heart: promise, rights, duties
cards.b:
"Salient features of the Constitution" is among the most repeated topics in Paper I Section B. Within it, the Preamble, Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are asked in many forms: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution? Has Article 21 become the most important right? Should duties be enforceable?

The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. It was adopted on 26 November 1949 after nearly three years of debate. It has 395 Articles and 8 Schedules at the start; it has now over 450 Articles and 12 Schedules.

Granville Austin, in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966), said its aims were threefold: national unity, democracy, and social revolution. Rights and duties show how it tried to join them.

cards.h: The Preamble: source, aims and status
cards.b:
The Preamble comes from Nehru's Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947). It begins "We, the People of India", showing that authority comes from the people.

Nature of the state

Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic. The words socialist and secular, and integrity, were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Objectives

Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity) and Fraternity (dignity of the individual, unity and integrity of the nation).

Status: In Berubari Union (1960) the Court said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it held that it is part, and amendable, but its basic features cannot be destroyed. LIC of India (1995) confirmed it is an integral part. The Preamble is not enforceable in court; it is an aid to interpretation.

Part III covers Articles 12 to 35. Article 13 makes laws that violate rights void, which is the base of judicial review. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a legal right under Article 300A.

Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. It lets anyone go straight to the Supreme Court.

Some rights hold against everyone (Articles 14, 21). Others, such as Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30, are for citizens only.

Article 14: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. It allows reasonable classification: the group must be based on an intelligible difference with a link to the law's aim. Reservations are an example.

In E.P. Royappa (1974), the Court said that equality is opposed to arbitrariness. Anything arbitrary violates Article 14. This turned equality into a tool for reviewing the fairness of state action.

Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, but allows special provisions for women, children, SC/ST and backward classes. 15(6) adds the economically weaker sections (103rd Amendment, 2019). Article 16 is equality in public jobs. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and Article 18 abolishes titles.

Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty "except according to procedure established by law".

  • A.K. Gopalan (1950): any procedure made by a valid law is enough. A narrow reading.
  • Maneka Gandhi (1978): the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a "golden triangle". This brought due process into Indian law.

Since then, Article 21 has covered the right to livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985), clean environment, health, speedy trial, and dignity. Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) made education a right for ages 6-14; the RTE Act followed in 2009.

K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 August 2017, nine judges) held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21. This led to rulings that decriminalised homosexuality (Navtej Johar, 2018) and struck down adultery as an offence (Joseph Shine, 2018).

cards.h: Freedoms under Article 19 and their limits
cards.b:
Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembly; association; movement; residence; and profession or business. Article 19(2) to (6) allow reasonable restrictions, such as for sovereignty, security, public order, decency and contempt of court.

  • In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Court struck down section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness and its chilling effect on speech.
  • Press freedom is read into Article 19(1)(a) (Romesh Thappar, 1950, and later cases).
  • The right to strike or to bandh is not absolute.

Articles 20 and 22 protect people in criminal law: no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, and rules on arrest and preventive detention. Preventive detention remains controversial.

Remedies under Article 32: writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. High Courts have wider writ power under Article 226.

The original Constitution had no duties. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IVA and Article 51A, on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, with ten duties. The 86th Amendment (2002) added an eleventh: a parent or guardian must give education to a child between 6 and 14.

  • Respect the Constitution, the flag and the national anthem.
  • Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle.
  • Uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity.
  • Defend the country when called.
  • Promote harmony and renounce practices that demean women.
  • Preserve composite culture; protect the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures.
  • Develop scientific temper and humanism; safeguard public property; strive for excellence.

Duties are not justiciable and carry no penalty by themselves. The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) suggested ways to give them effect. Courts use them to interpret laws and test whether restrictions on rights are reasonable.

• Too many limits? Critics say restrictions on liberty, such as preventive detention and sedition (now replaced by section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force from 1 July 2024), dilute rights.
  • Duties debate: Supporters say a rights-only constitution makes citizens passive. Opponents say duties were added during the Emergency to strengthen the state, and enforcing them risks authoritarianism. Many scholars see them as moral guidelines.
  • Positive vs negative rights: Part III is mostly "freedom from" the State. The Directive Principles ask for "freedom to" through welfare. Courts have joined them (see next lesson).
  • Enforcement gap: Article 32 is powerful but slow, and the poor have limited access.
  • Private power: rights bind the State, but private actors such as companies and platforms also affect rights. Courts have begun to extend some rights to private bodies.

• Climate: in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (21 March 2024), the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21.
  • Digital access: in 2025, the Court read access to digital services as part of Article 21 in a case on KYC for acid-attack survivors and persons with visual disabilities.
  • Speech: Shreya Singhal's principles guide cases on online speech. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) replaced the IPC.
  • Personal liberty: bail rulings emphasise "bail, not jail", including in cases under the UAPA and PMLA.
  • Data: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 followed Puttaswamy.
  • Equality: 2024's Davinder Singh and the EWS case show the court balancing Articles 14, 15 and 16.

Structure: Objectives Resolution to the Preamble; Berubari to Kesavananda on status; list of rights with Article 13; Article 14 and arbitrariness; Gopalan to Maneka to Puttaswamy; Article 19 limits; duties with the 42nd and 86th Amendments; critique; recent cases (climate, digital access).
